title: 2023 - Reconstruction of Trajectories of Athletes Using Computer Vision Models and Kinetic Analysis - Gan et al
file_name: 2023 - Reconstruction of Trajectories of Athletes Using Computer Vision Models and Kinetic Analysis - Gan et al.md
universal_lens: Monocular computer vision integrates 2D pose estimation with kinematic physics to reconstruct 3D athlete trajectories under affine projection assumptions. The lifting operator defines a non-linear mapping from the projective plane to Euclidean space, recovering latent 3D kinematic states. This structural unification bridges 2D pixel-space observations and physical trajectory reconstruction, establishing an isomorphism between visual manifolds and biomechanical phase spaces.
gsi_mapping: GSI employs conformal predictive inference on pose-derived kinematic features to generate probabilistic trajectory forecasts with uncertainty quantification. GSI treats the MHFormer lifting process as a Bayesian posterior inference over joint configurations. Conformal prediction bounds are applied to the lifted 3D coordinates, quantifying epistemic uncertainty arising from monocular depth ambiguity and ensuring robust probabilistic calibration of athlete pose estimates.
gse_mapping: GSE applies Bayesian belief updates over state-transition graphs of athlete motion to enable real-time tactical decision-making from reconstructed trajectories. In GSE, the lifted 3D skeleton serves as the discrete state vector for situational reasoning. Transitions between consecutive frames define kinetic state-flows, allowing the engine to simulate future trajectories and evaluate optimal movement vectors under dynamic environmental constraints.

reasoning_traces.think: The mathematical foundation of reconstructing athlete trajectories from monocular footage relies on resolving the inherent ambiguity of projecting a 3D Euclidean world onto a 2D projective plane. Standard 2D Human Pose Estimation (HPE) algorithms like OpenPose operate exclusively within the image manifold, yielding pixel coordinates devoid of metric depth. As highlighted in the text, this creates a fundamental disconnect because the camera image plane is rarely parallel to the physical trajectory of the athlete. To bridge this gap, we employ a 'lifting' operator, mathematically conceptualized as a non-linear mapping function $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^{2N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3N}$, where $N$ is the number of skeletal keypoints. The MHFormer architecture implements this mapping by leveraging temporal coherence and learned anatomical priors to infer the missing z-axis (depth) information. Once the 3D skeleton is reconstructed, the transition from pose to trajectory requires defining a continuous center of mass (COM). The authors approximate the COM by treating the human body as a linked-segment system, utilizing midpoint approximations for limbs and established mass percentages. This reduces the high-dimensional pose space to a singular kinematic point representing the athlete's global translation. Crucially, this derivation rests on strict physical assumptions: a flat ground plane and non-sliding feet. These constraints act as regularization terms in the optimization landscape, anchoring the estimated 3D coordinates to real-world metric scales. Without these boundary conditions, the lifted poses would remain invariant to arbitrary scaling and rotation relative to the ground. Thus, the entire pipeline transforms noisy, perspective-distorted 2D pixels into a rigorous, metric-compliant 3D kinematic state vector suitable for downstream quantitative analysis.
